Should anyone care?  Many are seeing is a failure vs Ramp, a measured success at best.  But … why?
I don’t think most people commenting on this actually understand what they’re reacting to. What they’re really feeling—even if they can’t articulate it—is the consequences of
hubristic fundraising
.

Hubristic fundraising is when you:
Take a valuation that requires Top 0.1%+ annual growth for a decade to grow into
Raise at 100x-500x+ revenue multiple.  Often, again and again.
Build your entire talent acquisition, press strategy, and customer pitch around being “the most valuable” or “fastest-growing”
Create expectations that anything less than a $20B+ IPO or massive strategic exit is a disappointment
These deals can work out.  It will work out for Databricks, Anthropic, etc.  But at least as of when I write this, there are so very few $30B+

last forever was clear to them.  So they tried to aggressively expand its platform by buying contact center leader Five9 for $14.7 Billion.  But at the time, the price didn’t clear, and Five9 shareholders turned it down.  Zoom’s phone product has been a material contributor for some time with 3 millions users, but it’s now pushing its own enterprise contact center and conversational intelligence products which are still early in their revenue ramp.  They’ll have success, but they got started too late to have a material revenue impact at $4B ARR.  It will take some time.

.  They grew faster than any other SaaS company in history after $1B in ARR.  But probably too fast, as CEO Eric Yuan often pointed out.  It wasn’t natural.  It was probably too much.  Zoom the app held up incredibly.  But they went from $1B to $4B ARR so fast, now they’ve got a little catching up to do as they move more enterprise.

answer: So we've all seen this movie before where companies that do well start to get out of their lane a bit too much. They think they're just like the hottest startups and maybe they have some good things going, but they don't really know how hard it is to keep up with the leaders at scale. But I'm surprised because one recent deal seems pretty egregious even by these standards, and that's Capital One buying Brex for $5.15 billion. And Brex had raised at a $12.3 billion valuation. That means Brex is selling for roughly half what they raised at. Now, Brex is still growing very quickly. So if they were able to sell at double triple digit growth, that would make sense. It might be worth more than twice what they raised at. But I bet it wasn't. Because there's a big difference between growing fast and growing hyper fast. If you look back at public software stocks today, the ones that can grow over 50%, 60% that have high margins are trading multiples of 10 times revenues, sometimes higher. The ones that aren't quite there trade at lower multiples. But none of them are at 300 x ARR. None of them are at 200 x ARR. Most importantly, none of them are at 700 x ARR. Which is exactly where Brex had been valued. Now, that does seem nuts now looking back. We'll see. Maybe they hit those valuations again. But it seemed nuts at the time. So my advice is, just remember that capital markets are unforgiving. A few months ago, AI agents were unstoppable. Today, Salesforce laid off 800 people. It's not all sunshine and rainbows. Make sure you understand why the market thinks your business is great.

answer:
So there’s no easy way to know exactly what happened here because all I have access to is this tweet:
Capital One announced today they will acquire Brex for $5.15 Billion
CEO & Founder Sam Blond announced his departure effective immediately
pic.twitter.com/FsQ9pNkFJt
— Myles Hatz (@M_Hatz)
February 10, 2026
It looks like it was $5.15 Billion.  That’s what Capital One said.  But Brex itself wasn’t clear.  It just said “terms were agreed” in a release.  We don’t really know yet if it was truly $5 Billion (with some cash), $5.15 Billion, etc.  Or even how much cash vs stock was involved.
What we do know is a few things … First, Brex had raised at $12.3 Billion pre-money valuations (Oct ’22) then fell dramatically during the downturn to < $1 Billion (!).  So whatever deal they got would likely be far lower than its peak valuation.
Second, it doesn’t look like anyone in the public markets thought Brex could get anywhere close to a $12B exit anymore.  Even at ~$600m ARR, getting even a $1B+ exit was probably seen by many as a stretch given current multiples.  The market cap of public companies doing similar things like Ramp, Navan, etc. aren’t trading anywhere near where Brex peaked at a $12B valuation.
Third, Brex isn’t the first startup to see the bar go up during the downturn.  And fourth, it shows how tough times can lead to founder departures.  Not always a bad thing per se, but often not fun for everyone.  A bit more on that
here
.
And a reminder that while VCs want founders who win, they also need them to survive long enough to have something left over for investors.  Sometimes that means letting folks go to focus resources on survival and growth.

answer:
So we've all seen this movie play out again and again across B2B. A startup raises a bunch of money at a crazy high valuation and then they get bought by a big tech company for … much less than the headline number. It happened with Bill.com, it happened with Clio, it happened with Veeva. And now I think it just happened again with Brex and Capital One. So what actually happened here?
Capital One announced an agreement to acquire Brex for roughly $5.15 billion. But if you dig into how that deal got structured, the actual story gets pretty interesting. Brex raised over a billion dollars at a valuation north of twelve billion dollars back in late 2021. This is where things start to go sideways because raising at such an extreme multiple means there's no margin for error. You're basically counting on top decile performance every single year for years and years. Fast forward to today, and the math doesn't work anymore. The company reportedly generated approximately $300 million in revenue in 2024. At even modest multiples, that would value the business well below the five point two billion announced purchase price. Now let me share something that might sound obvious but bear with me because it matters. When companies like this sell early – whether through acquisition or IPO – founders often frame it as "winning" regardless of the ultimate financial outcome. They'll say they created hundreds of millions in wealth for employees, investors, and themselves. They'll point to their legacy, their impact on the market, their ability to attract top talent. All those points are valid. But the reality is more complicated.

answer:
So we've all heard this one before, right?
Another unicorn bites the dust. Another startup just sold too late. Maybe even didn't sell early enough, maybe should have waited another year. But here's what I think most folks miss about these stories.
And what you're really seeing with Wrike now -- which had a great run. It was worth over $6 billion when it was acquired by HCL Technologies. We talked about how many times they almost got acquired. They finally did get acquired for $1 point something billion.

answer:
So what happens with this cap table when we're going out to raise again?
Well first, you're gonna hear all sorts of different answers from VCs, especially from seed stage VCs.
Some will say, "Oh, well, it doesn't really matter."
And then some will say, "I don't want to do anything with them because they just did something terrible like they gave away too much equity."
But here's my take after seeing so many founders go through this:
It matters less if you haven't raised since that crazy deal happened, but it still matters a lot if you've been raising since.
In fact, I would advise against anyone raising any new capital ever after having done one of these crazy deals.
Once you start raising, once you have a clean cap table, no one wants to see a big chunk of the ownership going somewhere else.
That's why I try to tell every founder I work with, "Just keep your cap table simple until you're ready to raise again."
Because you'll get more offers, you'll get more interest if there aren't weird things in the cap table.
This is true with any type of financing, whether it's debt or equity.
No investor likes to see their dollars being used inefficiently by dilution outside of the company.
Especially venture capitalists, who need to make sure that every single share that gets issued goes into their pockets in order to create liquidity.
So yeah, you know, that's my advice.
And also, I think a related piece of advice is never, never, never run out of money.
Never let yourself fall into a position where you're default dead without a term sheet in hand.
There are exceptions, right?
Like if you have enough cash that you're confident you could cut costs dramatically and extend your runway.
But most VCs won't invest in companies they feel are default dead.
They'll pass.
Even though they might think you're great, they just won't fund someone whose runway is zero days.
Or close to it.
So I always tell folks, you gotta be careful running out of money.
It leads to bad decisions. It creates chaos. And ultimately, it ends up killing startups.

Q:
How does a messy cap table affect future investors and fundraising?
A messy cap table can make fundraising harder because it shows investors that the company doesn’t value itself very high. This can also lead to lower valuations and less interest from potential investors. It’s generally easier to raise capital if you have a simpler ownership structure. And no one wants to invest in something where they think their investment won’t appreciate much.
______
And a few bonus questions:

#1 What would happen if I had to do a bridge round after my last fundraise?
The minute you’re default dead without a term sheet in hand, you’re in crisis mode.  In fact, most VCs just assume every startup will need another round of venture financing, and plan accordingly. But bridges aren’t free and rarely done by insiders that want to pay up.  So yes, bridges are possible.  But they take a lot of pressure off finding a solution faster.  And you likely need to cut your burn rate ASAP.  At some point, there’s almost nothing left to borrow against.

answer: The thing I love most about investing early stage startups is how much fun you get to have with each one. It's like having an option on your kid, right? And so, we all want our kids to do great things. We don't care what they end up doing, but hopefully, they'll make us proud. You got different types of investors out there. There's different stages. But here's the one thing everybody wants their kids to do is grow big. They just want them to keep growing. That's why you're excited. And if everything goes according to plan, this is where it gets interesting because you've got to go raise more money. You start off raising seed money, then you raise series A, B, C, D, whatever. It keeps going. So, if everything works, eventually you might even sell your company for billions of dollars, which means your parents will become billionaires overnight. Now, the thing that complicates this whole process is something called dilution. Dilution happens every time you raise another round of funding. So let me explain it. If I were to buy five percent of your company today and your company was worth say, $100 million, then my stake would also be worth five percent times $100 million, which equals $5 million. The problem is, later, you decide you need some extra capital. So you decide to raise another round of venture financing, but you ask the new investors to pay a lot less per share than what I paid. This means I'm left holding shares of your company that aren't worth very much anymore. In fact, I'd lose my entire initial $5 million investment. My ownership percentage hasn't changed, but my paper value has dropped to almost zero. To avoid losing millions of dollars on your company, you could try to convince existing shareholders to invest again.

If your cap table isn’t well-documented or up-to-date, it creates uncertainty. Future investors will want to see a clear picture of who owns what, and any ambiguity can delay or derail a deal.

answer: So there was an interesting discussion on our Twitter / LinkedIn this week on whether CEOs need to be hands-on in their business, or if they can just sort of manage and have the best people under them report up to them. And I don't know how you feel about this, but my experience is the folks who end up failing the most are ones who get more and more distant from the product itself. They spend all day meeting with customers and building out teams and doing strategy and working on marketing plans for years. But then they're never really involved enough in the daily operations to actually ship the thing. This makes sense according to the pilot data we collected. The data showed us that in 50 SaaS companies studied by the Stanford professors, those that stayed true to their original vision were far less likely to fail than those who got sidetracked by short-term gains. It’s hard to measure this exactly. But intuitively, one would think so. So when I see a CEO hire a bunch of VPs early, without ever having even been a VP themselves … that worries me. When I see someone join the board of directors of a company before they’ve truly built something themselves … that worries me. There are exceptions, clearly. But generally speaking, I worry a bit when I see too much distance between the founders’ passion and the reality of the business. Because ultimately, as CEOs, we’re judged on results. Not relationships. And the pilots tell us that staying connected to your why—your core mission—is critical to success. As the research shows, CEOs who remain authentic and engaged with their team and customers are less likely to lose sight of their purpose. They’re more resilient during challenges, better equipped to make tough decisions, and ultimately build stronger organizations.

Executives who stay close to the craft win, while those who become pure managers and strategists lose. As you scale, there’s always a temptation for execs to step back and let others handle the day-to-day details. But if you’re going after truly innovative markets like AI, staying close to customers and product development is often where the magic happens. Remember when most folks got laid off at scale-ups during Covid? Yes, it was rough. But also … everyone went remote. And it became clear quickly which ones could thrive without the office. Those were the ones that stayed closer to their customers. Now many of us want to go back to offices, but the same dynamic holds true today. Folks that really get the value proposition and can solve problems better tend to perform best in sales and engineering. They don’t just manage people well — they sell themselves. answer: So I did want to step back on this because one thing we know is almost everyone in B2B software now wants to use AI to personalize the customer experience more than ever before. We talked to an incredible CMO recently who literally just left her job, she'd been running marketing at a very successful unicorn for years. She came out swinging in our podcast like she hasn't seen anything better than ChatGPT for personalization. That's how excited she is. But what does that really mean? Is every single interaction with your product going to have to be personalized? Can they all be done through a chatbot and a prompt? A lot of folks think so. So I wanted to see if I could find where this first originated. It seems like such a great idea. Everyone loves personalization. They're good at it when they have lots of humans and can do it manually, but even there, customers complain they don't get enough attention. What would happen if we could magically deliver that to each and every customer, no matter how small, no matter how large, with a prompt? The originator here I believe was the founder of Rippling, Parker Conrad. He wrote a pretty interesting article on his thoughts on the future of enterprise SaaS after attending SaaStr Annual. He gave us some great content. He had some great insights. One of them was, "I've decided the future of business software is to make it hyper-personalized." Now, I'm sure many of you love the word "hyperpersonalized" because it sounds cool. But actually, it's probably already been achieved by many of your competitors. Rippling's vision here is that AI will allow companies to build exactly what customers want -- customized workflows, tailored experiences, and automated processes all without needing to code.

answer:
Who said that AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience?
Anneka Gupta
AI will also have a personalization layer on top of it so we can talk to it like ChatGPT or Claude where I don't know every single feature in Asana so if I say "I want to track my time better" it would understand what I mean and make some suggestions to help me do that versus just saying "Hey here's how you use the timer."
What does that look like in practice? Well, there is this concept called "intents." So, when you're using the app, you'll tell it what your intent is, and then the system will go through different pieces of code that try to fulfill those intents. That way, you won't need to navigate through multiple places. It'll just take care of it for you. The second piece is more around understanding who your users are, which we've talked a lot about, right? How do you really get to know them, how do you really personalize for them? Because right now, you're talking to a persona, not a real human being. There are so many personas in a company. There are 500 people. You might think that one team uses Slack, another team uses Microsoft Teams, and they all use something else. But actually, everyone uses Slack because they don't even know anything else. They just use whatever tool is available to them. So, making sure that our products deeply understand who our customers are and why they buy us, why they choose us over others, is super important.

answer: So we've got some interesting questions here. Let me just quickly summarize them before I answer because there's actually two questions. One of 'em really kind of gets at the root of what folks want out of AI in B2B software which is who said this "AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience"? And then another question is around NRR and driving it down. So let's start with that first question. The reason this matters is we had a bit of an internal debate on our little team when I put this up on LinkedIn. There were a bunch of people that I think would disagree with Anneka who made that point. I don't know if she'd even agree herself anymore, but she did say it pretty recently and I found it quite provocative. It suggests that every interaction with your app should be personal. Not just your top customers, but everyone. That seems like maybe too big of a ask. And so my sense is that's probably true, but that's also a bit of a cop-out. Because the real question is how do you get it done? Can you make your free edition feel like it's truly worth $10,000? Or can you make your smallest customers feel they're getting something similar to the service, attention, love, care, whatever you call it that a $100k deal does get? A lot of us struggle with that. We have a few thoughts, though. First, one thing that we see a lot of startups doing wrong is trying to sell more than what they deliver.

And so I looked it up. It turns out there are actually two tweets with this exact same quote, one from April of this year and another from November of last year. So here we have our speakers.
Anneka Gupta, head of product for Gorgias, and Jason Lemkin, founder of Saastr. And I'm going to summarize these two different versions of this tweet because they're pretty great. But first let me ask you what do you think? Am I wrong? Is this something that everyone's talking about in B2B right now? Because if you look around, I don't really see people saying like, "We need to make everything super personal."
Maybe I just haven't seen enough stuff yet. Maybe I've been too focused on my tiny little world of AI agents. But maybe it's all coming soon.
So let me tell you why this matters, which is the AI revolution is changing how we build software faster than almost any time in history. We're building new products in weeks instead of quarters. The pace of change is unprecedented. But with all the excitement, there's also confusion. What does this mean for your business? How should you approach this rapidly evolving landscape?
Let's break down these key points that Jason brought up. First, AI doesn't have to be expensive. You don't need a large team of engineers. There are many tools available today that enable rapid deployment without breaking the bank. Many startups started off open source and then built commercial solutions. You could use ChatGPT and Claude to figure things out.

answer: So my general advice on hiring a new VP of Sales is this: - First ask if they can truly hit plan in 90 days with just their small team (not including any internal resources). If they can't — pass. They don't really understand your business. You need someone that can get you to first $Xm faster than now. - Next, ask how many quota-hitting reps they've directly managed before. And make sure those quota-hitters were individual contributors / SDRs >and< closers. Not just "managers" or people that didn't close anything themselves. If they haven't hired at least 1-2 strong quota-closing reps for real themselves... then I doubt they ever did. - Finally, ask what % of their revenue was closed by folks that worked for them directly. Ask for the number. It almost always turns out < 50%. So no matter how much talk there is here -- the best VPs of Sales hire folks that already know how to sell the product. But importantly, that's often just 25%-30% of their team. The rest of their team is made up of folks that want to learn how to sell the product. This ratio usually changes over time, as the company grows and scales. At some point, most of the sales team will have been trained by folks that used to report to the VP of Sales. answer: So I've talked on SaaStr for years now about hiring a great VP of Sales. How to hire one. What mistakes you make when you don't hire a good one. But there are two issues that sort of pop up with a lot of folks who get it wrong. And they're related, and we'll talk about both here. One is the idea if you have a stretch VP of Sales — maybe she came from a very different industry, a very different type of product, whatever it might be — that somehow it's bad to criticize him if you don't see improvement over time. It's too early. It's just too hard. You got to back her. If nothing else, your board won't support her if she can't show improvement. They'll lose confidence if they think this isn't going to work. So what do you do? Well my advice is don't go out of your way to criticize someone that hasn't performed yet. Even though many times you feel like it. My advice is don't go out of your way to criticize anyone until their performance improves. Because even if they didn't perform well before, if you start criticizing them after they join, that will almost never help anything. Most people will quit right then and there. Now if they were already doing terribly, maybe you need to make some changes. But once again, most people know ahead of time if they're really failing. Then they leave. So let me tell you a story. This was a CEO I worked with recently. He hired his first real VP of Sales ever. His VP of Sales had sold at Box, which is a great company, but selling at Box is totally different than selling to startups, especially in the beginning. Selling to companies like Facebook, Google, Amazon, Netflix, et cetera, versus selling to little startups. Totally different products.

answer: There is no point doing anything less than perfect when you hire your VP of Sales. It's just too important. So if they don't hit the plan their first month, fire them. If they aren't recruiting strong folks under them by Month 2, fire them. If they can't close every big deal themselves -- even when they lose -- by Month 2, fire them. And importantly, criticize them mercilessly until then for failing. Because most won't deliver, period. They'll blame others. Blame marketing for lack of leads. Blame product for being feature poor. Blame anyone else except for themselves for not hitting the plan. But what you really need to do is help them succeed. Help them get there. This is also why I've never made this mistake myself hiring sales leaders. We all make mistakes. The key isn't making fewer mistakes (you're going to). It's knowing how to learn faster from those mis-hires. And learning what to look for after each one. You have to know what worked before, and what didn't. At least, for the next iteration. answer:
So I've worked with so many different VPs of Sales over the years, and maybe you have too, and there's just two types. There's a mediocre VP of Sales, and then there's a truly great VP of Sales. And here's what I know:
The mediocre ones do almost nothing except complain, criticize others for not doing well enough
[...]
And they don't really try to make anyone else better than them. The mediocre ones tend to like to hire folks underneath them that aren't quite as good as them, but kind of similar. They're afraid if they bring in someone smarter, better, more experienced, something else, that that'll threaten their job.
A mediocre VP of Sales focuses primarily on process
[...]
They take a lot of time talking about how things should happen, talking about goals, making sure every single goal gets met by every individual. It's very important to set clear goals, but they spend way too much time focused on process. Instead of going out there and helping your team close those big deals, instead of jumping into the tough deals yourself and figuring out why they lost, instead of hiring some of those amazing people ahead of you. You see this all the time with mediocre managers. They sort of focus on the future. They sort of focus on how we need to get better next year, which is true. But they don't go out and help us win today. So again, let me contrast these two. If you can't step up as a VP of Sales, if you haven't hired some real quota-hitters before, if you haven't done it, don't blame others. Don't point fingers. Don't say "it was the economy" or whatever it is. Blaming others won't solve anything. What solves everything is when you hire a few truly great reps and a few truly great sales leaders.

answer:
Criticizing a VP of Sales who cannot do better is counterproductive
https://t.co/8cYlOq0HkV

As I’ve shared many times on SaaStr over the years, hiring a “wrong fit” VPS can end up costing you almost as much as if you’d never hired anyone at all.  If they don’t work out, and you just let things slide … it’s hard to get back to where you were before.
But what happens when your new VPS does OK — for a while? But then doesn’t really grow your revenue anymore?
Should you criticize him or her, point fingers, make demands? Or will that hurt morale even further? I.e., can you ever move forward past this stage?
I’m not sure there’s a simple answer. Let me share my learnings here:
First, some bad VPs of Sales will take advantage of time. They’ll promise to hire their top reps, but won’t actually do so. So yes, they’ll look good initially — at first. Then later, they’ll have zero people left underperforming. Which often looks even worse than before. Don’t play these games. It always ends badly. Instead, find someone else to replace any failing sales execs asap. Second, sometimes it’s best to just agree to disagree on performance issues. Sometimes, a VP of Sales will push back on how many leads she needs per rep, or how big an ACV she can close, etc. There’s nothing wrong with pushing back against an unrealistic goal set by management. But it also doesn’t help if you argue too much here. Instead, just agree on goals that are achievable given the current state of the company. Third, don’t expect miracles from a mediocre VP of Sales.

answer: So I've talked on SaaStr for years now about hiring a great VP of Sales. How to hire her. What mistakes you make when you don't find a good one. But there were two points that we didn't dig into too much. And so let me just quickly summarize those today because they're super important if you haven't figured this out yet. Number one, don't criticize your VPS. Don't tear him apart over the internet. If she can't get it done, then move on. But don't criticize her publicly. Because that is almost always counterproductive. It undermines their confidence. It undermines morale. In fact, most VPs will quit after public criticism. So instead, what you need to do is backfill him. Help him. And if you have to go another month, you'll survive. Your revenue will still grow. It won't kill you. But tearing someone down doesn't help anyone. Number two, folks want to know whether or not a great VP of Sales needs to bring in all these reps under them. Can they really do it alone? Well, yes and no. Yes, if it's early stage, maybe start off with just one rep yourself. Maybe even zero. If it's later stage, well then probably you need three to four reps in the first week or two. And a VP of Sales that wants to work themselves up from nothing, well, they might be able to do that. They might want to put in the effort. But that's rare. It's very hard to do it without any experience. And ultimately, if you want to scale faster than 10x, you're going to need to hire ahead of time. We've also learned since Covid that folks aren't as interested in working remotely anymore. Many VPs of Sales, many CROs want to manage reps in the office. They want to fly around.

I’ve seen it again and again across 30+ investments, 10+ unicorns, and hundreds of portfolio company board meetings.
There’s one pattern that predicts VP failure better than anything else I’ve seen. Not their resume. Not their pedigree. Not even their interview performance.
It’s whether they still do the actual work themselves.
Let me break this down by function, because the pattern holds true across every C-level and VP role:
CROs Who Don’t Sell
Every time I see a CRO that doesn’t sell themselves, they fail.
Not “occasionally jump on calls.” Not “review deals at the end.” I mean actually carrying quota. Actually running discovery calls. Actually negotiating contracts. Actually closing deals.
The best CROs I’ve worked with—the ones who took companies from $5M to $50M+ ARR—never stopped selling. They’re in the CRM. They’re on calls with enterprise prospects. They’re working the biggest deals in the pipeline.
Why? Because the moment you stop selling, you lose:
Feel for what’s actually working in the market right now
Credibility with your team (they know when you can’t do what you’re asking them to do)
Ability to coach effectively (you’re coaching from theory, not practice)
Understanding of where the real bottlenecks are in your process
I’ve watched CROs who were “too senior” to carry a bag struggle to diagnose why conversion rates were dropping. Meanwhile, their quota-carrying counterparts could tell you exactly which objection was killing deals because they heard it three times that week.
CTOs Who Don’t Code
Every time I see a CTO that doesn’t code themselves, they fail.
And I don’t mean writing trivial scripts or reviewing PRs from a distance. I mean actually shipping features. Actually debugging production issues. Actually understanding the codebase deeply enough to make real architectural decisions.
